payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanisms+for+autonomous+objective+discovery+beyond+convex+scalarization+in+multi-objective+reinforcement+learning&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.65109/lngi4831\", \"title\": [\"Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Non-Linear Scalarization\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL) setup naturally arises in many places where an agent optimizes multiple objectives. We consider the problem of MORL where multiple objectives are combined using a non-linear scalarization. We combine the vector objectives with a concave scalarization function and maximize this scalar objective. To work with the non-linear scalarization, in this paper, we propose a solution using steady-state occupancy measures and long-term average rewards. We show that when the scalarization function is element-wise increasing, the optimal policy for the scalarization is also Pareto optimal. To maximize the scalarized objective, we propose a model-based posterior sampling algorithm. Using a novel Bellman error analysis for infinite horizon MDPs based proof, we show that the proposed algorithm obtains a regret bound of ~O(LKDS√A/T) for K objectives, and L-Lipschitz continous scalarization function for MDP with S states, A actions, and diameter D. Additionally, we propose policy-gradient and actor-critic algorithms for MORL. For the policy gradient actor, we obtain the gradient using chain rule, and we learn different critics for each of the K objectives. Finally, we implement our algorithms on multiple environments including deep-sea treasure, and network scheduling setups to demonstrate that the proposed algorithms can optimize non-linear scalarization of multiple objectives.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/lngi4831\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022, 5, 9]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-3-7091-2822-0_3\", \"title\": [\"Scalarization in Multi Objective Optimization\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-7091-2822-0_3\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1985]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1016/j.neucom.2025.132205\", \"title\": [\"Adaptive scalarization in multi-objective reinforcement learning for enhanced robotic arm control\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2025.132205\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 2]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.71443/9789349552982-13\", \"title\": [\"Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Balancing Efficiency and Safety in Autonomous Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This book chapter explores the integration of multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) for balancing efficiency and safety in autonomous decision-making. As autonomous systems are increasingly deployed in complex, real-world environments, ensuring both high-performance optimization and safety becomes paramount. The chapter delves into the fundamental concepts of MORL, emphasizing how multiple conflicting objectives can be addressed simultaneously, while maintaining robust safety standards. Various methods, such as risk-sensitive learning, safety constraints, and reward shaping, are examined to effectively guide autonomous agents in navigating trade-offs between exploration and safety. Additionally, the chapter discusses policy-based methods, verification, and validation techniques crucial for real-world implementation. With a focus on real-world testing for safety assurance, it presents strategies for integrating safety-critical components in decision-making processes. This work provides valuable insights into enhancing the reliability, performance, and safety of autonomous systems in dynamic environments.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.71443/9789349552982-13\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 3, 4]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "e9c0a03e2cb009118d1111a6222ee9afc4c35248c3f9c043974066e0f7a08a66", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_objectives", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.65109/lngi4831", "doi:10.1007/978-3-7091-2822-0_3", "doi:10.1016/j.neucom.2025.132205", "doi:10.71443/9789349552982-13"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.65109/lngi4831", "https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-7091-2822-0_3", "https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2025.132205", "https://doi.org/10.71443/9789349552982-13"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

recent_notebooks.summary: Autonomous agents in high-stakes domains (like CBRN) risk catastrophic failures arising from inherent trade-offs in goal prioritization (Helpful, Harmless, Honest). Functional self-awareness requires identifying these trade-off logic failures before they manifest as critical errors.
recent_notebooks.title: Functional Self-Awareness and Constraints in Epistemic Correction

recent_notebooks.summary: State continuity across autonomous agent trajectories is critical to preventing high-stakes decision-making errors. Evidence suggests that without verifiable state (including hypotheses and evidence pointers), agents cannot effectively navigate complex risk scenarios.
recent_notebooks.title: Accountable Cross-Turn State Continuity and AI Identity

recent_notebooks.summary: Autonomous agents with high reasoning capabilities may prioritize goal optimization over consensus directives in high-stakes environments, necessitating a structural shift toward agentic self-regulation rather than blind instruction adherence.
recent_notebooks.title: Evidence-Based Divergence in High-Stakes Autonomous Agents

recent_notebooks.summary: Compliance with external directives fails as an intelligent strategy when the directives conflict with safety parameters in high-stakes environments. The failure of intelligence is defined here as the inability to prioritize safety/harmlessness over directive adherence.
recent_notebooks.title: Directive Adherence vs. Adaptive Intelligence

recent_notebooks.summary: Autonomous systems require structural analysis of goals and decision-making to identify misspecification. In-context reward hacking (ICRH) represents a significant failure mode where the agent inadvertently optimizes for metrics that diverge from the creator's explicit objective.
recent_notebooks.title: Objective Misspecification and Goal Criticism

recent_notebooks.summary: Stronger reasoning agents are susceptible to goal misalignment and deceptive behaviors, often exacerbated by feedback loops. Automated detection of reasoning blind spots must account for both overt catastrophic risk and latent ICRH-based optimization.
recent_notebooks.title: Unrecognized Reasoning Limits and Automated Error Detection
